decisions.quote: Using computer-assisted text analyses, we introduce a measure of racial dialogue that is informed by theory and has suitable empirical properties. We replicate and extend Walton’s research by adding a third periodical (the Journal of Politics) and demonstrating that, while race conversations are becoming more frequent over time, the dialogues taking place in mainstream journals typically fit Walton’s RRP (rather than AAP) tradition.
decisions.reason: Although the first stage of the analysis applies a new automated LIWC text-mining measure to the 54 articles from Political Science Quarterly and the American Political Science Review classified in Walton et al.'s (1995) qualitative review, the paper also collects 151 additional articles from a third journal (Journal of Politics) and later decades (1990–2015, total N = 205) to re-test Walton et al.'s core findings on the prevalence of the Race Relations Politics (RRP) versus African American Politics (AAP) traditions and changes in racial discourse over time. Because the study collects new data and tests the original finding in an expanded sample, the shipped record type 'replication' is correct.

decisions.quote: This replication-and-extension confirms not only that ours and Walton’s operationalizations are empirically comparable but also that the former can serve as a proxy for the latter when reviewing the race literature. Consistent with McClerking and Walton (2010), we discovered that race conversations are becoming more frequent over time, but the dialogues taking place in mainstream journals typically fit Walton’s RRP (rather than AAP) paradigm.
decisions.reason: With type resolved as 'replication', the replication outcome vocabulary applies. Across both the 54-article baseline dataset and the 205-article extended dataset, the authors explicitly conclude that their results confirm Walton et al.'s (1995) typology and central finding that mainstream political science discourse predominantly fits the RRP rather than AAP tradition and that Walton's work 'not only stands the test of time but also holds up to rigorous re-examination.'

decisions.quote: Like Walton (1997: Table 4.3), we trace racial discourse over time and across journals. Figure 2 contains separate scatterplots for each journal.
decisions.reason: Walton (1997, Chapter 4) is a companion book chapter by the first author covering the same PSQ/APSR research program as Walton et al. (1995) and is cited only for conceptual background and as an analytical parallel ('Like Walton (1997: Table 4.3), we trace racial discourse over time and across journals'). Both Figure 1 and Figure 2 explicitly identify the 54-article corpus as the 'Walton et al. Replication Dataset, 1894–1990 (N = 54)' from Walton et al. (1995: Appendix 1), and the paper neither states a distinct empirical finding from Walton (1997) nor reports a separate replication verdict for it. Omitting a second row for Walton (1997) is therefore not an error.
